claims.text: Replacing EAM+TI with a DFT-trained MTP+FEP workflow for TaVCrW will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP+FEP workflow will maintain sub-meV free-energy accuracy.
Accurate FEP requires the MTP to reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution of the complex liquid at 2000-2400 K.
The TaVCrW initial state is a disordered BCC solid solution at 0 K.
A compositionally related W-Ta-Cr-V alloy exhibits chemical SRO and a tendency toward Cr-V-rich segregation.
Solid-state SRO contributes approximately 2-3 meV/atom of stabilization energy.
The MTP must capture local atomic environments and Warren-Cowley SRO parameters to reproduce solid-phase stabilization.
An MTP can serve as a computationally efficient DFT surrogate while retaining sufficient accuracy for complex solid and liquid phase-space sampling.
Accurate MTP phase-space sampling enables FEP to compute the solid-liquid free-energy difference without the slow convergence of TI.
An inaccurate or overly rigid reference potential can cause TI to miss the SRO stabilization contribution.
The MTP training set must include representative TaVCrW liquid configurations at 2000-2400 K and solid configurations containing SRO.
A supercell containing more than approximately 200 atoms is needed to avoid finite-size suppression of the proposed SRO stabilization energy.
The supercell must resolve an SRO correlation length of approximately 10-15 Å.
The predicted melting temperature from MTP+FEP will be within 10-20 K of the TOR-TILD result.
Electronic excitations can shift the calculated melting temperature by tens of kelvin.
The MTP+FEP solid-liquid free-energy difference will deviate from the TI baseline by less than 0.5 meV/atom.
Empirical GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules do not hold for V and Cr at 0 K, potentially propagating error into the MTP.
Neglected high-temperature magnetic fluctuations may significantly alter TaVCrW phase stability or melting behavior.
The proposed method should be benchmarked against TOR-TILD on a simpler refractory alloy using matched melting-temperature, free-energy, cost, and SRO measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if the free-energy discrepancy exceeds 0.5 meV/atom or if cost reduction is below 80% while melting-temperature agreement within 20 K is maintained.
